title: Ascension
summary: The Gospel passages listed here do not narrate one identical ascension scene. Luke closes with Jesus blessing his followers and being carried into heaven, although wording in Luke 24:51-52 varies among manuscripts. Matthew ends with a commission and John with resurrection appearances; neither passage describes the same departure. Mark 16:19 says Jesus was taken up, but it belongs to Mark's longer ending, textually distinct from the earliest recoverable ending at 16:8. These differences matter: ascension language connects resurrection with Jesus' exalted status, while each Gospel frames its ending in its own way.
historical_context: Historically, Ascension is located by its canonical setting; this entry connects that setting with jesus, messiah-theme, new-covenant and related CKL objects for contextual retrieval.
ancient_near_east_context: Ascension unfolds within concrete settings such as Israelite kinship life, temple worship, royal courts, wilderness travel, Roman administration, or imperial conflict, depending on the passage.
literary_context: The cited Gospel endings are related but distinct: Luke narrates a departure, Matthew closes with a commission, John recounts resurrection encounters, and Mark 16:19 appears in the longer ending. They should not be blended into one uniform scene or chronology.
covenantal_significance: Across the cited passages, the risen Jesus is linked with divine authority, mission, and witness. The accounts express these themes differently, and not every passage listed narrates an ascension.
canonical_role: Luke closes with an ascension scene and Acts opens by revisiting Jesus' departure; Matthew, Mark, and John preserve related but differently framed endings. This event therefore links resurrection with the disciples' continuing mission while keeping each Gospel's account distinct.
